transcript:
Meeting header
Date/Time: 2025-10-07T15:00:00Z
Duration: ~42 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: yes
Attendees: Jared Park (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Carlos Rivera (CTO - Pinecrest), Leah Kim (Platform Eng), Samir Patel (Security)

Summary:
Rapid discovery to scope a Private/VPC deployment of Redwood for Pinecrest's analytics platform. Primary concerns: static egress IPs for allowlisting, VPC peering vs PrivateLink, region constraints (AP-Southeast presence), data residency/GovCloud considerations, routing and NAT/firewall architecture. Next step is a hands-on network workshop and sharing security docs.

Topics discussed:
- Private deployment options: provider-managed control plane vs customer-controlled control plane
- VPC peering, Transit Gateway, and AWS PrivateLink tradeoffs
- Static egress IP / NAT / Elastic IPs for allowlisting vendor endpoints
- CIDR overlap concerns across multiple accounts and workspaces
- Logging, KMS/HSM key ownership, SSO/SAML, SOC2/ISO requirements
- Timeline and success criteria for pilot (latency SLAs, data residency)

Audio transcript (timestamps approx every 20-40s, transcription imperfect):
[00:00] Jared: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, Jared from Redwood. We'll keep this focused — Maya and I are the AE/SE pair. Carlos, Leah, Samir, thanks for taking time.
[00:16] Carlos: Yeah thanks. We're trying to understand what the network setup would look like if we run Redwood Private in our AWS accounts. Want to know what we need to open, what IPs to allow, and how routing looks.
[00:28] Maya: Great. Quick high-level — we support a few patterns: direct VPC peering from your VPC to a Redwood-managed VPC, PrivateLink (interface endpoints) to the control plane, or we can deploy the full private stack into your VPC (customer-managed nodes). Each has different requirements for egress and routing.
[00:45] Leah: Okay, so what's the difference operationally? We're heavily segmented — infra in 3 AWS accounts, some overlap in CIDRs is already an issue.
[01:00] Maya: Right. VPC peering requires non-overlapping CIDRs. If you have overlaps, PrivateLink or a Transit Gateway with NAT/inspectors is usually the pattern. PrivateLink gives you a stable interface endpoint per region and avoids CIDR overlap but you need to set up interface endpoints and security groups.
[01:20] Samir: Our security team will not let outbound IPs be ephemeral. We need to allowlist static egress IPs for the model calls to any external systems and also for Redwood control plane callbacks. Do you provide fixed egress IPs?
[01:35] Jared: Short answer: we can provide a small range of static egress IPs for dedicated/private deployments via NAT gateways or egress proxies. If you use Redwood-managed egress we'll publish the Elastic IPs; for customer-managed deployments you can force egress through your NAT/Firewalls so nothing leaves your routing controls.
[01:50] Carlos: Are those IPs per-region? We have strict rules: EU traffic must stay in eu-west-1, APAC in ap-southeast-1. We can't have calls egressing to us-east-1.
[02:05] Maya: We can pin control plane and data plane deployments by region. The egress IPs are region-specific unless you choose multi-region routing. For Pinecrest's requirement, we'd suggest deploying the Private workers in the same region as the data — that keeps traffic local and matches latency and residency needs.
[02:22] Leah: How about cross-account peering? Our infra team wants Redwood nodes in a central shared services account, not every team account. Is that supported?
[02:36] Maya: Yes, common pattern: we place Redwood workers into a shared account VPC and peer into consumer accounts. You need a peering/transit gateway in place and route table updates. If you have Transit Gateway we can attach to it as well. For account boundary security we recommend separate security groups and strict route tables.
[02:52] Samir: CIDR overlap again — we have two developer accounts that accidentally use 10.0.0.0/16 and 10.0.0.0/16. That blocks peering.
[03:06] Jared: That's where PrivateLink helps — because it uses ENIs and interface endpoints, no peering route updates, and no CIDR non-overlap requirement. The tradeoff is more interface endpoints to manage and per-endpoint costs.
[03:20] Leah: About costs — will PrivateLink be noticeably more expensive? We run many small calls, high QPS.
[03:30] Maya: PrivateLink has per-GB and hourly endpoint costs. For high-throughput, dedicated peering or Transit Gateway can be cheaper. Also Redwood Optimize can batch requests or prefix-cache to reduce total egress. We'll show cost comparisons in the proposal.
[03:48] Carlos: We also have a downstream data lake that only accepts traffic from certain static IP ranges. If Redwood nodes initiate any calls to S3 or our Egress endpoints, we need those IPs to be known up front.
[04:02] Maya: If you host the workers in your account they will use your NAT or egress IPs. If we host them in a Redwood-managed VPC, we can provide the Elastic IPs to allowlist. For Redwood-managed with peering, you can add a firewall rule to accept traffic from that peered CIDR and then we manage the NAT.
[04:22] Samir: Audit and key management — we need to know where keys live. Do you support customer KMS/HSM keys for model encryption and storage?
[04:35] Jared: Yes, for Private we support customer KMS for data at rest. For control plane or shared offerings, keys are Redwood-managed, but we can run an enterprise contract allowing BYOK (bring your own key) in certain configurations. We also have HSM integrations for higher FIPS requirements.
[04:51] Carlos: SAML/SSO integration — we use Okta. And we need RBAC down to team level.
[04:59] Maya: We integrate with SAML/OIDC and support SCIM provisioning and role-based access. In Private deployments you control the identity store and can map groups to Redwood roles.
[05:14] Leah: Any special route table changes? Our infra team is sensitive about route propagation.
[05:24] Maya: For peering, route table entries to the peered CIDR are needed. For PrivateLink you create interface endpoint ENIs in the subnets you choose — no route table edits apart from enabling DNS resolution. For Transit Gateway, you attach VPCs and propagate routes to a central RT; that depends on your TGW policy.
[05:41] Jared: Also note NAT and SNAT behaviour — if you care about the source IP preserved, you need to run in your account or use egress proxies that support source preservation. Many customers route egress through an appliance (e.g., Palo Alto, Fortigate) to enforce DPI and logging.
[06:00] Samir: Speaking of logging, we need VPC Flow Logs and audit logs forwarded to our S3 bucket for retention 7 years. Can Redwood push logs or do we pull?
[06:12] Maya: Best practice is to enable VPC Flow Logs in your account so logs are owned by you. For Redwood-managed VPCs we can optionally stream flow logs to a bucket you own via a cross-account role. Application-level audit logs (API request logs) can be forwarded through an HTTPS ingestion to your syslog or to a storage endpoint, subject to deployment mode.
[06:32] Carlos: GovCloud — a subset of our customers are US gov contractors and data must live in GovCloud partitions. Do you support deployments in GovCloud or other isolated partitions?
[06:42] Jared: We do support GovCloud and isolated regions with an enterprise Private deployment. It typically requires a separate contract and dedicated infrastructure; we can provision nodes in the GovCloud region and use customer-owned networking. We'll need compliance paperwork.
[06:58] Leah: What's the typical timeline for a pilot? We want to validate latency (p50/p95) and run a small workload.
[07:07] Maya: A pilot can be 2-4 weeks. First week is network setup and access, second is basic workload testing and perf benchmarks, third is tuning (batching, quantization), fourth is ramp and docs. For your scale, estimate ~3 weeks to meaningful metrics.
[07:22] Carlos: Latency targets — we want sub-200ms token wall for short completions in region. Is that achievable?
[07:30] Maya: If you host workers in-region, yes. For hosted cross-region, you'll see extra hops. We'll share benchmark data; our dedication with GPU pools gives predictable tail latencies.
[07:43] Samir: Data retention on our side — are model-context logs stored anywhere outside our control?
[07:50] Jared: For Private/customer-managed, context and logs stay in your account/cluster. For Redwood-hosted, we have retention controls and can opt-out of storing prompts. We can sign data processing terms to ensure no model training on your data.
[08:06] Leah: Network-level question — do you require route propagation to be enabled on Transit Gateway? We have strict conservatism there.
[08:16] Maya: Not required; you can manage route tables manually. Deployment will follow your governance. We generally prefer explicit routes but can plug into TGW propagation if that's easier for you.
[08:30] Carlos: Let's talk concrete port numbers and endpoints we need to allow.
[08:36] Maya: Control plane uses HTTPS over 443 to specific FQDNs; we'll provide a list. For model-serving traffic, depends on design: if we deploy worker pods in your subnets they make outbound HTTPS calls to your internal services or S3. If using peering, ports are standard TCP 443 for API traffic. For PrivateLink you'll need to allow interface endpoint ENIs and the AWS-managed range. We'll send a checklist.
[09:00] Jared: One catch we see — some customers block all egress except through a proxy that does TLS interception. That breaks certificate pinning. If you have TLS-inspection we'd need exceptions or in-cluster egress that bypasses interception for service-to-service traffic.
[09:18] Samir: Good note. We do use a corporate TLS proxy in certain accounts. We'll identify which accounts that is.
[09:25] Leah: Any known gotchas with EKS networking or CNI plugins? We use Calico in some clusters and AWS CNI in others.
[09:34] Maya: Both are fine typically. For Calico with IP-in-IP or overlay networking, be mindful of MTU and fragmentation when using PrivateLink or inter-account peering. We'll ask for your CNI configs in the workshop.
[09:47] Carlos: Can we keep model artifacts inside our S3 and have Redwood pull them?
[09:54] Maya: Yes, you can store model weights in your S3 and we can reference them via IAM roles or cross-account role. We support ECR and private registries for container artifacts too.
[10:05] Jared: Let's talk a little about support model and SLA. For Private deployments we offer enterprise SLAs on uptime for worker nodes if you pick Dedicated or Reserved capacity. For fully customer-managed nodes, support is cooperative — we are on-call for the Redwood layer, you manage infra.
[10:22] Samir: For our procurement, we need a network diagram that shows peering, subnets, and CIDR allocations. Can you produce that?
[10:29] Maya: Yes, we'll draft a few patterns: (A) Redwood-managed VPC + peering, (B) PrivateLink to Redwood control plane, (C) full customer-managed workers in your VPC. We'll include route tables and NAT placement.
[10:42] Carlos: What about egress through our firewall — can traffic from Redwood nodes go through our transit firewall?
[10:49] Maya: If workers are in your account and subnets are routed through Transit Gateway and your firewall, yes. If workers are in Redwood-managed VPC, we can peer and route through an egress connection but some customers prefer local workers to stay within their security boundary.
[11:03] Leah: Who owns certs for mutual TLS? We use mTLS in some internal APIs.
[11:09] Maya: We support mTLS for service-to-service connections. For PrivateLink, it sits at the network layer, you can enforce mTLS at application layer. Certificate management generally stays with the party terminating TLS — so you can provision certs in your side, or we can coordinate for shared endpoints.
[11:24] Carlos: Any requirements for IAM roles? We'll need a cross-account role for Redwood to assume to push logs?
[11:31] Jared: Yes, commonly we ask for a cross-account IAM role with restricted permissions for S3 write or CloudWatch put events. For security we use least privilege. We'll give a CloudFormation snippet.
[11:43] Samir: We should talk about encryption keys — you mentioned BYOK. Do you rotate keys automatically?
[11:49] Maya: With customer KMS keys you control rotation schedule. For Redwood-managed keys we rotate per our security policy and provide rotation logs. With HSM you get hardware-backed key protection.
[12:00] Carlos: Anything else we should think about for the pilot that often surprises customers?
[12:06] Jared: Two common surprises: 1) CIDR overlap blocking peering — have your network team audit CIDRs early; 2) corporate egress proxies breaking certificate trust — identify interception early. Both are cheap to fix if found in discovery but expensive mid-pilot.
[12:21] Leah: Good to know.
[12:23] Jared: Okay, shifting to timeline and next steps — we propose a two-hour network workshop next week with your infra and security folks, send the security pack and a detailed network checklist, and then identify a single AWS test account for the pilot.
[12:37] Carlos: That works. We'll invite our network lead and operations.
[12:42] Samir: We'll want to review SOC2/ISO artifacts before starting.
[12:47] Jared: We'll attach those. Link to Redwood security page: https://redwood.inference/security (redwood placeholder). Also we'll share a private-deploy checklist doc: https://redwood.inference/privatedeploy-checklist.pdf
[13:03] Maya: For the workshop we'll draft sample CloudFormation and TGW attachments and a PrivateLink endpoint example; we'll also prepare a short perf-runbook to collect p50/p95 data.
[13:15] Leah: Anything on the contract side? Costs for dedicated IPs and Transit Gateway?
[13:21] Jared: We'll include estimates in the follow-up quote — breakdown for worker hours, egress IP allocation, PrivateLink per-endpoint costs, and an optional reserved capacity discount if you commit.
[13:33] Carlos: Ok. Recap us the main risks and what you need from us.
[13:38] Jared: Risks: CIDR overlap preventing peering, corporate TLS proxies breaking flows, GovCloud/legal constraints for certain datasets. What we need: VPC diagrams, CIDR lists, list of accounts that must remain in-region/GovCloud, point-of-contact for network and security.
[13:55] Samir: We'll provide that.
[14:00] Leah: One minor — we need to know if your control plane will ever call out to external telemetry endpoints. We need to vet domains.
[14:08] Maya: Control plane telemetry is HTTPS to our endpoints; we have a whitelistable set. For Private you can choose telemetry opt-out or self-hosted metrics forwarding. We'll mark that as an action.
[14:21] Jared: Great. Any final questions?
[14:25] Carlos: No, this was helpful. We'll look at schedules for the workshop.
[14:29] Jared: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the security pack, network checklist, and a proposed workshop time.

End of transcript (recording truncated for clarity).
